In her letter replying to my account of the misadventure, she wrote: “Dear George, please try to be easier on yourself, a better friend than you have been. Don’t be ashamed of limiting the demons, of avoiding them if possible. Don’t be ashamed of finding some new purposes there so that you will be able to achieve/perform/be comfortable with yourself.”

What else could a frightened mother say? You’re not your father—don’t do what he did. But this pleading to go back to who I was before seemed dangerous. Anyway, it was too late.

At Christmas I traveled through Burkina Faso to Europe for a short visit. In Barcelona everything went wrong. The faces in the Museu Picasso were so grotesque that I could hardly look at them. The girl I had come to see didn’t know what to say to me. One day, I resisted an impulse to jump in front of a city bus and realized that, if I went back to the village for my last six months, I probably wouldn’t make it. For a year and a half I had been barely hanging on.

In an English-language bookstore, looking for something to read on the plane back to the States, almost at random I bought a Penguin edition of Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia. The cover image showed a bolt-action rifle with brass cartridges, a crumpled red flag, and an old Spanish newspaper. I knew nothing of the Spanish Civil War, and I knew Orwell only as the author of 1984, a book assigned in high school. I hadn’t read any of his essays, or any writing of that kind at all. I had never thought of nonfiction the way I thought of novels and poems—as literature.

Crossing the Atlantic I was overcome with a sense of utter failure. By leaving early, I had failed my students and friends in the village; and everyone back home, above all my mother; and most painfully I had failed myself. Disgrace and defeat were written on my face, and I avoided eye contact with other passengers. I felt that at 23 I would have to start over, with no idea how.

I opened my book and began to read: “In the Lenin Barracks in Barcelona, the day before I joined the militia, I saw an Italian militiaman standing in front of the officers’ table.”

Something about this sentence struck me: its lack of fuss, its plainness and strength, the way “I” led quickly and easily to a scene, a view of the world. As I read more, the book started to give me courage. This might be a way of going on: by facing the truth and getting it all down, simply and clearly.

First I had to face my mother. In the house where she had raised me, full of the books that had made me want to be a writer, we mostly avoided the subject of why I was home early. Instead, at dinner that first night, we got into an argument about literature. We were talking about Heart of Darkness, one of the books in which I’d searched for answers by kerosene lamplight. My mother thought that the narrator, Marlow, was kept sane by his devotion to work and duty—by repression. To me, Marlow could avoid Kurtz’s fate only by immersing himself in Kurtz’s madness. Of course, we were talking about why I was home early, and what it meant for me, for us. My mother spoke gently, with none of the old sparring, because she knew that she stood to lose something precious. I argued with growing fury, as if not just a literary disagreement but my whole life was at stake.

Forty-one years later, as my mother lay dying in the same Stanford hospital where I’d been born, she emerged from dementia long enough to squeeze my hand and tell me: “I love you. I’m proud of you. Now go on about your business.” But that night in January 1984 she was still trying to hold on to the boy she had made. At last, as if admitting defeat, she said: “I thought you were steel tempered in fire.”

That was the last time we spent more than a few days together. I went to Boston, for no good reason, and found a job on a construction crew. In the evenings after work, I sat at the Olympia manual typewriter that had gone silent in Africa and started to write. I wrote about the village, and I wrote about my father.

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Sons and Mothers.”

entries.title: ‘Feminism Is the Consequence of the “Man Problem,” Not Its Cause’
entries.summary: Readers respond to our June 2026 cover story and more.
entries.content:
Readers respond to our June 2026 cover story and more.

The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote

Helen Lewis argued in the June issue.

Helen Lewis’s “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” is the most important thing I have read this year. My husband has said that Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election because of the misogyny that exists in America; Lewis’s article proved him correct, with just a teaspoon of humor mixed into an otherwise very frightening topic.

Amy Crist

Gettysburg, Pa.

Upon finishing “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote,” I found myself equal parts stunned and galvanized. Lewis has an extraordinary ability to illuminate what so many of us feel but struggle to articulate, and this article was no exception.

The MAGA movement contends that feminism is to blame for American decline. But feminism didn’t emerge from nothing. Feminism is the consequence of the “man problem” Lewis identifies, not its cause.

The Bible passage that anti-feminist commentators love to cite is from Ephesians: “Wives, submit to your husbands.” But that’s where they stop reading. The verse goes on to say that a husband must provide for his wife, and love her as he loves his own body. This is not a “do as I say or else” arrangement; it is a covenant of mutual care—her health and happiness are meant to be as important to him as his own, and vice versa. When men forget the instruction to care for their wives as they care for themselves, women have no choice but to learn to care for themselves.

I was recently at the pharmacy, and the man ahead of me—trying to pick up a prescription for his sick wife—answered the pharmacist’s questions with “I don’t know; my wife takes care of that.” When a husband utters, “My wife takes care of that,” the word that means “everything.” It means knowing the passwords, the medications and dosages, the appointment schedules. It means knowing what to say to assuage a teenager’s broken heart, whom to call at the school, how to manage a crisis. It means caring for sick husbands and aging parents—sacrificing for the people you love.

I am the breadwinner in my family. My husband stayed home and raised our three daughters. The plan was for him to return to work once the girls were in elementary school. But we all know what happens when we make plans—God laughs. My husband now lives with a neurological condition that complicates our lives in ways neither of us anticipated. Does working to provide health care for my children and husband make me less of a woman? Would my husband be mocked in the manosphere for not working? Is staying home to raise children noble only when a woman does it?

Erika Jackson

Gilbert, Ariz.

I worry that “The Men Who Don’t Want Women to Vote” misses a crucial component of the rise of masculinism. I stand in vocal opposition to misogyny and the idiocy of the far-right masculine media sphere. I teach my daughters that they control their bodies and that they should never miss a vote. But I do think that a large cohort of men is struggling with issues that have been ignored, or sometimes even mocked, by the mainstream media. Many men try to be good husbands and parents, only to hear mantras like “We don’t need men” and “There are no good men out there”; on social media, people discuss whether they’d prefer to be trapped in the woods with a man or a bear. Meanwhile, American men are nearly four times more likely than women to die by suicide. The manosphere discusses that issue frequently, as Lewis notes; the mainstream media do not. When men hear negative messages about being a man from the mainstream media but see the manosphere addressing their struggles, they will gravitate toward it. I hope society can learn to address male issues without mocking them. Otherwise, I fear, the extremism will continue.

Ben Rodriguez

Suffield, Conn.

A significant number of men are never fully socialized. These men have few if any friends—and certainly no female friends. Deep down, they may not hate or fear women; they just don’t know how to interact with them. They never learned how to work with or cooperate with them. If one accepts that, then quixotic attempts to repeal women’s suffrage or strip women of social and political freedoms should not surprise anyone.

Virgil Jose

Apple Valley, Calif.

Helen Lewis makes a convincing argument that the noisy, often lewd misogyny of the MAGA right is no longer fringe and presents a real danger to women. This sexist worldview reflects and interacts with patriarchal systems across the world.

Examining more than 350 variables across 176 nations, the scholars Valerie M. Hudson, Donna Lee Bowen, and Perpetua Lynne Nielsen have demonstrated that “the fate of nations is tied to the status of women.” Their 2020 book, The First Political Order: How Sex Shapes Governance and National Security Worldwide, shows that nations that subordinate women tend to be more fragile, autocratic, corrupt, and impoverished. The subordination of women appears to produce the kind of governance that leads to worse outcomes for everyone. The sexual political order is, as they write, the “first political order”—what starts in a family shapes a broader community’s politics.

Eleanor H. Klauminzer

Olalla, Wash.

Helen Lewis replies:

As you might imagine, this article prompted a large and varied mailbag. I heard from grandfathers—happily married for decades—who couldn’t understand how society seemed to have gone backwards, from middle-aged men who felt overlooked because their problems weren’t fashionable, and from parents who worried about what their sons were watching online. I came away thinking that screen-time limits are good, that schools should do more to accommodate rambunctious boys as well as conscientious girls, and that the Democrats need to develop their own, positive visions of masculinity to compete with those of Andrew Tate and Nick Fuentes.

Some of the likely 2028 presidential contenders have started to do that: Gavin Newsom talks regularly about men’s problems, and signed an executive order aimed at improving mental-health services and reducing male suicide rates in California. Pete Buttigieg has learned how to bro out on podcasts such as Andrew Schulz’s Flagrant—the kind of spaces where Donald Trump did so well during the 2024 campaign. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez waded into the debate over the looks-maxxer Clavicular (the guy who claims to have achieved a better jawline by hitting himself with hammers) by highlighting the pressures on young men to conform to unrealistic beauty standards. The conversation is definitely shifting.

Behind the Cover

In this month’s cover story, “Empire of Grift,” Anne Applebaum examines how hardened ideologues and opportunistic profiteers are bending American diplomacy to advance an antidemocratic agenda—and their own financial interests. For our cover, the illustrator Ben Hickey created an ominous image of figures in shadow arrayed around a map of the world, evoking the war-room scenes from Stanley Kubrick’s 1964 film, Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb.

Corrections

“The Great Romance Slump” (September) stated that birth control was legalized for married couples in 1965. In fact, in 1965 the Supreme Court held that the government couldn’t restrict a married couple’s access to birth control. “Confessions of a Token Black Professor” (September) described a sign affixed to the wall of a former mill in Lewiston, Maine, as neon. In fact, it is a marquee sign.

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “The Commons.”

entries.title: What Comes After America
entries.summary: Emily St. John Mandel’s latest work of science fiction considers the tenuousness of any possible future.
entries.content:
Emily St. John Mandel’s latest work of science fiction considers the tenuousness of any possible future.

Emily St. John Mandel writes science fiction, with the accent firmly on fiction. Imagination, not technical verisimilitude, is her strength; she wisely disregards the scientific in favor of the human. Her indifference to plausibility is a measure of her confidence as a storyteller, and helps snare readers like me, who have a mild allergic reaction to postapocalyptic settings and outer-space odysseys. Her previous novel featured time travel, interplanetary travel, and a cosmic glitch; now, in her challenging new novel, Exit Party, we have accidental teleportation between parallel universes. The underlying theme, though, is irresistible: how shockingly little humanity understands about the sudden swerves and reversals that shape a life—or end it. The new book also offers a prescient invitation to consider the human toll that a world of chaos or repression can exact.

Exit Party’s stunning first sentence leaps ahead to 2031 and peeks into a woman’s soul: “In the first spring after the collapse of the United States, the blossoming of the jacaranda trees felt to Ari like grace.” Newly released after 18 years in prison, 48-year-old Ari Waker is just getting used to a Los Angeles that has seen vicious internecine violence. Although international peacekeeping troops have been withdrawn and the city’s curfew has been lifted, nothing like normalcy prevails. Ari walks with her roommate from their apartment in Echo Park (note the locale) to a party in Silver Lake. There, the incomprehensible happens: Two people from a parallel world materialize at the party, and another person (the host) is teleported in the opposite direction—all by accident.

The inexplicable appearances and disappearances are as disorienting for the reader as they are for Ari, who wonders whether she has a brain tumor or is having a stroke. For the three teleported individuals, the experience is a disaster: instant, complete, and irreversible dislocation. In the alternate universe, we soon learn, the “United State” has become a fortress, “closed like a fist,” where the national doctrine is “Harmony at any cost.” There we encounter, among other characters, Ibari, an enforcer of the brutally repressive social order.

Abrupt cataclysm is a signature of Mandel’s recent work. Before Exit Party came Sea of Tranquility (2022), The Glass Hotel (2020), and Station Eleven (2014)—all of them ingeniously splintered narratives involving many protagonists, zigzagging timelines, and some kind of shattering event. It’s never clear until the end that the shards of narrative can be assembled to form a coherent story. The big picture that at last emerges in Exit Party features paired life stories of doppelgängers, genetically identical sets of characters who have made decisions in their divergent worlds that move them along radically different paths. Ari and Ibari are the principal “twins.” Though at first they seem utterly dissimilar, they are, as Ibari recognizes late in the novel, “two sides of the same coin.”

Repeatedly drawn to criminality (which she associates with freedom), Ari has had more than her share of “hinge moments,” the term she prefers for dramatic, world- and life-changing twists. She launched one criminal enterprise—selling luxury goods bought with stolen credit-card numbers—as a teenager, while living in Brooklyn with an aunt and uncle who dealt in stolen antiques. Soon enough, helped out by her cousin, she was selling U.S. passports. When the Russian Mafia lured her into smuggling people, her cousin, beset by moral qualms, balked. So she hired an assassin to kill him. That’s how she landed in prison.

Sprung from jail and hoping to find her footing, Ari drifts instead. She works as a dishwasher and in warehouses, and then becomes, in dizzying succession, a gunrunner, a trophy wife, a philanthropist, an art collector. Arriving in Paris in a car with bulletproof windows (another hinge moment), she wonders, “How many completely separate lives am I going to get to live before I run out of chances.” Mandel makes this resilient character—a serial transgressor with a pragmatic code of ethics, uncannily accurate premonitions, and a touching capacity for regret—sympathetic and compelling. Her last name, Waker, is a clue to her essence: She’s awake, aware. She will always notice the jacarandas.

A meticulous observer by profession, Ibari is 79 when we meet her, and has risen to a high rank in the Internal Security Service. She’s as frank about her complicity in the disappearance of rule-breaking fellow citizens as Ari is about her weakness for criminality. Ibari has nonetheless imagined a scenario in which, instead of running surveillance operations for the State, she became a criminal; like her twin, she felt there would be “freedom in that.”

The door that swings open at the party remains thereafter obdurately shut. Appalled, puzzled, fascinated, Ari and Ibari (in their parallel worlds) try their best to comprehend what has happened. They investigate, quizzing the accidentally teleported. Eventually, they (and the befuddled reader) learn enough about each other and the different worlds they inhabit to have some thoughts about “entanglement”—about how doubles in their respective universes intersect. Which they do, eerily. Even before she knows anything about Ibari and her career in the secret police, Ari wonders why she herself hadn’t “just become a detective, instead of turning to crime.” She can see the appeal of a life played out in the ranks of the NYPD. She yearns for a homeland where she would be spared the “permanent unease” of encroaching anarchy, where armed fighters aren’t forever shooting at one another on the edge of town.

In Exit Party, those who diverge nearly converge, and every echo resonates.

When they were young girls, Ari and Ibari each read the same children’s detective novel and both latched on to the same sentence: “True diligence means following the improbable path.” While in prison, Ari had TRUE DILIGENCE tattooed on her left wrist; to judge from the improbable path that Ari and Ibari’s creator has followed, it’s Mandel’s motto too.

After growing up in western Canada, mostly homeschooled, Mandel graduated in 2000 from the School of Toronto Dance Theatre. Nine years later, at 30, having abandoned her dream of dancing professionally, she published her debut novel. Like her next two books, it was a noir thriller; all three slipped by more or less unnoticed. Her fourth, Station Eleven, about a flu pandemic “that exploded like a neutron bomb over the surface of the earth,” killing almost every human, won prizes and much-deserved critical praise, and sold remarkably well—before getting a big bump six years later during COVID. Sales of the book passed the 1 million mark shortly after the first episode of an HBO adaptation aired, in late 2021.

Station Eleven was Mandel’s own hinge moment. In addition to introducing what has since become her fiction’s hallmark fracturing of time and lives, the novel displayed her calm authority and her easy way with ambitious imaginative gambits—one world erased, another fighting to be born—carried off with barely a trace of writerly flourish: “The caravans had once been pickup trucks, but now they were pulled by teams of horses on wheels of steel and wood.” In Mandel’s work, unadorned realism is at the service of baroque invention, and everything, including the prose, is subordinate to the story.

Like all the best stories, hers are character-driven. In Station Eleven, Kirsten Raymonde, a child actor before the pandemic and afterward a skilled warrior, is canny and resourceful in the face of catastrophe. Eight years old when her familiar world ended, and a semi-feral teenager when she hooked up with a ragtag troupe that stages Shakespeare plays and orchestral concerts, Kirsten is permanently traumatized, ferocious when necessary, and somehow still capable of tenderness. She’s a sturdy hook for the reader.

Mandel holds tight to some of her characters: She teleports a few between the parallel worlds of her novels. Ari made her debut in The Singer’s Gun (2010), where she was already mercilessly pragmatic and minimally sentimental. An important prop in the new novel is a painting by a minor but vivid character in The Glass Hotel, Lucas Alkaitis, a heroin-addicted artist, talented and doomed, “on the run from mediocrity and Brylcreem and grey flannel suits.” Lucas himself also reappears, still an addict, still committed to his art, in a curious coda to Exit Party set in his Manhattan studio in 1960—a final, wrenching narrative swerve.

In Sea of Tranquility, you’ll find a Mandel stand-in: a newly famous writer in the year 2203 who has left her moon-colony home for planet Earth to embark on a globe-spanning book tour. Separated from her family, she finds herself unmoored, homesick. An interviewer in Estonia asks her what it’s like to have published a tremendously successful book. She answers, “I wrote three books that no one noticed, no distribution beyond the moon colonies, and then … it’s like slipping into a parallel universe.” She continues, “I somehow fell into a bizarre upside-down world where people actually read my work. It’s extraordinary. I hope I never get used to it.”

One of the projects of modernism (and postmodernism) is to unsettle our confidence in the coherence of the self and thereby reveal the truth about our disjointed identity, so often sabotaged by an unruly unconscious. The so-called neomodernist novelist Rachel Cusk has declared that she is “not interested in character because I don’t think character exists anymore.” It seems to me that Mandel, who merrily jettisons narrative conventions and plays cunningly with timelines, nonetheless insists on the essential coherence of her fictional creations. How many completely separate lives can Ari live and still track as a character? “I took out a contract on my cousin,” she says to the host of the Silver Lake party. “It was a mistake and I’m not that person anymore.” I don’t believe her. Though she probably would not now pay to have a close relative murdered, she remains the ruthless person who once did.

All of the doubling that powers the plot of Exit Party prompts us to consider how we recognize ourselves and others—whether we believe in the integrity of our persona and theirs. What is the essential stuff of our identity? What makes us whole? In The Singer’s Gun, Mandel has Anton Waker, the cousin Ari thought she wanted dead, provide an answer: It’s details, “small and personal and utterly beautiful and mundane, that make up the fabric of a person’s life.” Hinge moments may matter less than humdrum daily doings. We change tack, break free, and start over, yet we carry with us the stubborn imprint of all our old habits, the jumbled storehouse of memory, and a long trail of sensory data so familiar that it goes unnoticed. We endure.

And we suffer, due to circumstances beyond our control. This is where the doubling of the radically different nations comes in. Which is less awful, the calm and sinister surveillance state that Ibari serves with growing reluctance, or the “fracturing continent” that Ari yearns to escape? At first Ari reacts to chaos with a rueful calm—“You don’t notice the supply chain till it collapses”—but after years of “flashes of gunfire at night” from militia skirmishes that “stopped just short of all-out war,” a bone-crushing weariness sets in. As she knows, “Societal breakdown is exhausting.”

The “malevolent weight” of a tyrannical government is similarly sapping. When the secret police is everywhere, Ibari wryly notes, “anyone can be surveilling you at any time, including the person whom you are yourself surveilling.” To live peacefully, you make believe everything’s fine, ignoring “black cars moving too slowly down sunlit streets, unsmiling plainclothes agents in pairs, drones gliding quietly through the air.” At the academy where she trained to join the secret police, Ibari was told, “A harmonious society comes at a price.” The instructor added, “And we are not just the ones who exact that price, we are the ones who pay it.”

Mandel declines to identify any specific ideology in either world. No dictator is referred to in the totalitarian regime; no feuding warlords are named in the failed state. In both places, the status quo has evolved without recognizable human agency. That’s simply how it is—for now.

Ibari comes to treasure the phrase “No country lasts forever,” because “there was such hope in that.” A bitter sort of hope, but one that chimes with the spirit of the novel as it winds down, attuned to fluid time as well as fluid space. With Edna St. Vincent Millay’s “famous little poem” about burning the candle at both ends in mind, the artist Lucas Alkaitis (soon to die of a heroin overdose) reflects, “The point isn’t that the candle won’t last the night. Everything is temporary. The point is that the light is gorgeous while it lasts.”

This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “What Comes After America.”

entries.title: A Night for Actor’s Actors, Not Movie Stars
entries.summary: This year’s Emmys ceremony celebrated versatile performers, not glitzy celebrities.
entries.content:
This year’s Emmys ceremony celebrated versatile performers, not glitzy celebrities.

When the Widow’s Bay creator Katie Dippold accepted her Emmy for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series last night, she joked that she was so proud of her win, she intended to display her trophy as prominently as possible in her home. The award would be mounted on a rotating turntable, she explained; mirrors would be set up around the space so that visitors could always see it, wherever they were. “This is going to become my entire personality now,” she warned.

This year’s Emmys essentially turned Widow’s Bay into its personality too. The Apple TV series about a haunted island town full of eccentric inhabitants swept the field, winning six categories over the course of the evening, including Outstanding Comedy Series. The show’s star, Matthew Rhys, even made Emmys history: With his win for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series, he became the first-ever nominee to score a trophy in all three lead-actor categories. (Earlier in the night, he was awarded for his work on The Beast in Me, a limited series; in 2018, he won for The Americans, a drama.) His achievements helped underline how much the ceremony honored true-blue actors such as him—and how television, despite years of movie stars dominating prestige shows, remains best designed for versatile performers and textured roles.

Consider Rhys’s fellow winners from Widow’s Bay, a series that marries the chill of a Stephen King novel with the goofy humor of Parks and Recreation. Kate O’Flynn, who built her career in British theater, won Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her spirited turn as Patricia, a lonely but resilient woman. Her co-star Stephen Root, who took home the trophy for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series, is widely regarded as an actor’s actor—the kind of performer who adds depth to any story, no matter the genre. In his speech, he underlined how unusual it was for him to be recognized, pointing out that his son was shocked that he was in the same category as Harrison Ford.

The ceremony, of course, featured plenty of movie stars: Michelle Pfeiffer, Nicole Kidman, Tom Holland, and Zendaya were all seated close to the stage. But many of the performers who took home awards were respected TV-industry veterans who have spent most of their career disappearing into their work rather than commanding the spotlight. Noah Wyle may now be an Emmys favorite after winning two years in a row for starring on The Pitt, but he beat out Mark Ruffalo and Gary Oldman for the honor. Allison Janney (who, to be fair, is an Oscar winner) expressed shock about winning her first Emmy in 11 years, for her arresting supporting turn as a fictional U.S. president on The Diplomat.

The night also featured several satisfying, overdue wins: Rhea Seehorn, who led six seasons of the often-nominated Better Call Saul, finally took home her first Emmy, for her jittery performance on Pluribus. Hiro Murai, a director who has helped define the cinematic look of modern television through his work on shows such as Atlanta and Barry, won his first directing Emmy, for—once again—Widow’s Bay.

The Emmys producers seemed to know that many of its winners might not be household names. The show was front-loaded with the performance categories, which meant that all of the acting awards were finished halfway into the three-hour show. That’s unusual for a Hollywood ceremony, which normally tries to keep people glued to the screen by showing as many stars for as long as possible, and boosting viewer anticipation for their speeches. But then again, the night’s host was Mariska Hargitay, one of television’s mainstays; she’s led the cast of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit for 27 seasons, with another on the way. To honor a slate of experienced pros felt only right.

entries.title: Jean Smart’s Reminder to the Women in the Room
entries.summary: The actor’s history-making Emmys win was a recognition of female performers who refuse to placate.
entries.content:
The actor’s history-making Emmys win was a recognition of female performers who refuse to placate.

The actor Jean Smart began her acceptance speech at the Emmys tonight with a request: “Just the men stay standing,” she said to the applauding crowd before her. “The girls get to sit down.”

She had just won her fifth-straight award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for her role on HBO Max’s Hacks, about the tender and testy friendship between an unfiltered comedy legend (played by Smart) and an apprehensive Gen Z comedy writer (Hannah Einbinder). As she clutched her statuette, Smart acknowledged the squeezing and taping and blister-inducing heels that had likely gone into her peers’ glamorous award-show getups. Her well-dressed colleagues in the crowd, she joked, must be muttering, “She’s not that good”—as in, not so talented as to merit a standing ovation that required maneuvering in uncomfortable gowns.

Landing that achievement for a character such as Vance feels particularly appropriate. Smart played her as a gutsy, hard-headed, and occasionally vulnerable elder statesman of comedy, who’d erected walls around herself in her fight to be taken seriously in a male-dominated medium. Her win, for a role that embodied the difficulties of being a woman who refuses to placate those around her, parallels her character’s arc; it also calls to mind how tough it is for someone like Vance to earn that level of industry success.

Smart, notably, was not the only actor honored this evening for playing an uncompromising woman. Rhea Seehorn, who took home the award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series, portrayed the fiercely self-reliant author Carol Sturka on Pluribus, whose stubbornness in a newly dystopian world is laced with grief. Kate O’Flynn won for her supporting role on the comedy series Widow’s Bay as Patricia, a government bureaucrat whose ill-advised attempts to fit in make her a town pariah. And Allison Janney clinched a Supporting Actress trophy for The Diplomat, on which she played U.S. President Grace Penn as a particularly shrewd political operator.

The actors who played these distinct characters are “linked, not ranked,” as Seehorn said in her speech, quoting the late Gloria Steinem—a nod to the women’s shared lineage as industry colleagues rather than awards competitors.

But Smart’s enduring charisma as Vance, and her character’s notable refusal to quit, also enabled her to make this history. In Season 1 of Hacks, much of the humor stemmed from the intergenerational mismatch between Vance and her new joke writer, Ava Daniels, who begin working together at an inopportune time in both of their careers: Daniels has been deemed persona non grata in Hollywood, while Vance is collecting checks from casino gigs in Las Vegas. Both of them eventually manage to find an uneasy rhythm together—but Vance’s professional drive, which often took precedence over the feelings of her closest collaborator, was the show’s engine.

Over the course of the next four seasons, Smart revealed Vance’s vulnerable side, even as her character kept up a steady stream of barbed commentary: In her many decades in the industry, Vance had huge opportunities wrenched from her hands—most dramatically her short-lived late-night show, which she spent decades striving for but ultimately abandoned amid studio pressures. But even that move was a testament to the comic’s devotion to her convictions, no matter how unpopular they might make her. By rewarding Smart several times over for this role, the Emmys seemed to recognize something deeper in her performance—and the worth of the woman she so impressively brought to life.

entries.title: The Supreme Court Recognizes the Danger of Trump’s Election Plan
entries.summary: A majority of justices decided not to make the coming elections needlessly more chaotic than they already are.
entries.content:
A majority of justices decided not to make the coming elections needlessly more chaotic than they already are.

Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night, nor Donald Trump will stop the United States Postal Service from delivering mail-in ballots in the coming midterm elections. Tonight, the Supreme Court handed down an emergency ruling blocking the Trump administration from implementing a new policy that would have made mail-in voting so onerous as to be effectively impossible for election officials to administer. The Court’s decision spares those officials from pointless chaos—and voters from potentially widespread disenfranchisement.

In the United States, election administration is carried out by a patchwork of local officials working state by state across roughly 10,000 different jurisdictions. Usually, USPS’s role in elections is clear: The Postal Service transports mail ballots to voters from state and local election offices; if voters return their ballot by mail, USPS takes care of that too. The nature of this responsibility has evolved in recent years, particularly during the coronavirus pandemic, as many states shifted toward encouraging voting by mail. The Trump administration looked at this system, which has been popular among voters, and decided to cause havoc by imposing new and arduous criteria for election officials to meet before USPS would commit to mailing ballots.

A number of states and several nonprofits, along with the Democratic Party, quickly brought legal challenges. Before the Court resolved the matter tonight, the cases zagged madly among district and appellate courts, then up to the Supreme Court and back down again. Many judges were skeptical both of the legal basis for the rule and of the speed at which the administration was attempting to implement it, with less than two months to go before the elections.

But despite this broad agreement in the lower courts, experts were uncertain how the Supreme Court would handle the case. The Court’s past friendliness toward even the most legally dubious of Trump’s policies cast into doubt whether the justices would stand against his efforts here, especially after the Court rejected an earlier iteration of the challenge on the grounds that it was premature. “The Supreme Court has made law totally unpredictable,” the election-law expert Justin Levitt told me last week, while the country waited for the justices to rule. “In a normal world, there would be a zero percent chance” that the Court would allow the USPS rule to go into effect. Yet, he went on, “we don’t live in a normal world anymore.”

Our world is still not a normal one. But this time, a majority of the justices on the Supreme Court decided not to make it worse. In a terse, unsigned paragraph, the Court declared that the Trump administration had failed both to make its case on the law and to show that a ruling in Trump’s favor would not upend the upcoming elections. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a brief concurrence, indicated that the Postal Service’s plan might have had firm legal grounding but that he’d agreed to block the policy because “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”

That final part of his assessment is obviously correct. USPS’s plan would have required election officials to upload lists of eligible voters through a Postal Service “portal”—yet the government has given no indication that the portal is operational. USPS would also have required election officials to receive Postal Service approval for the design of their ballot envelopes, but officials have already printed their ballot envelopes and do not have the money or time to create new designs. Last week, a Tallahassee, Florida, paper reported that USPS had rejected the envelope designs submitted by Florida’s Leon County on the grounds that the return address was 0.014 inches too close to other text on the envelope—about the thickness of four sheets of paper.

Election administrators prepare to send out ballots far in advance, and if the USPS rule had gone into effect, election officials might have found themselves unable to count on the Postal Service to mail ballots at all. However conservative the Supreme Court is, “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos,” Levitt wrote to me after the ruling.

Still, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, the pair on the Court who most reliably tilt toward Trump, would have allowed the USPS plan to go forward. Alito’s dissent is strikingly unconcerned with the potential risks to the midterms if the Postal Service were to refuse to mail ballots, noting only that 12 states (all Republican-led) have “asserted that compliance at this time is practicable.” (Local election officials in some of those states disagreed with that assessment in their own court filings, but Alito does not address this.) Moreover, the federal government’s interest in detecting “election fraud” is compelling, Alito declares. As for the last-minute dash to shake up the midterms, Alito manages to blame not the government but the plaintiffs, the lower courts, and even his own colleagues on the bench for the litigation that—he claims—delayed USPS from finalizing its rule.

In a blog post, the UCLA law professor and election scholar Rick Hasen deemed Alito’s dissent “disingenuous.” Among other things, USPS continued working on the rule during the course of the litigation over the summer. And even if the Postal Service had finished the planning process earlier in the summer, state and local jurisdictions still might not have had enough time to rework their envelopes to comply.

Fortunately, officials won’t need to scramble to submit envelope designs to USPS to be measured down to fractions of an inch, or upload voter names into a portal that doesn’t exist. Election workers will likely face plenty of challenges in the month and a half before the midterms. Mailing ballots, though, will not be among them.

entries.title: ‘The Flood is the Point’
entries.summary: As the midterms approach, the president can’t stop picking fights.
entries.content:
As the midterms approach, the president can’t stop picking fights.

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Donald Trump loves a deal, even if, at times, it’s just the idea of a deal. The president’s trade dispute with Canada continues to drive one of America’s closest allies into a closer relationship with its chief competition. Although Trump is insisting that “Canada wants to make a deal very badly,” there is very little evidence that’s true, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney—enjoying broad national approval for his combative response to the American leader—looks to strengthen its alliances in Europe and Asia.

Meanwhile, AI leaders are publicly calling for a slowdown. That was the gist of the message delivered by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this weekend in an essay warning that the technological advances of AI are outpacing the ability to ensure that they are safe. His concerns were echoed by some of the biggest names in tech—OpenAI leader Sam Altman and Elon Musk.

But the president saw something else in their warnings: “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Trump wrote on his social-media site this morning.

This week on Radio Atlantic, my colleagues Ashley Parker and Tom Nichols join me to discuss the president’s trade war with Canada, the Trump-centric Republican midterm convention in Dallas, and whether an aging Congress can regulate AI.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Ashley Parker: To be somewhat fair to Trump, or to anyone, is that this is just fundamentally incredibly complex. If you’ve ever watched these members of Congress—which is basically a gerontocracy—try to get to the bottom of Snapchat or Instagram or social media with teens, right, it’s like they’re speaking a foreign language, and those are table stakes, right? AI is a million times more complicated than posting a problematic video on YouTube or Instagram.

Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris. Congress is back on Capitol Hill for the last time before the midterm elections, and they have a lot to think about—the burgeoning trade war with Canada and warnings from tech CEOs about the dangers of unregulated AI, among other things.

And when those lawmakers return to the campaign trail for the final stretch, the ones in competitive districts may have some company—members of the president’s Cabinet.

With me to discuss the news of the week are my colleagues Ashley Parker and Tom Nichols. Let’s get to questions.

Welcome to the show.

Parker: Thanks for having us.

Tom Nichols: Thanks, Adam.

Harris: Ashley, I want to start with you because you had a story that ran recently about something that people I think have become a little bit desensitized to, and that’s the potential violations of the Hatch Act, which limits the partisan political activities of federal employees. You and our colleague Michael Scherer reported on a competition among the Cabinet secretaries to travel to competitive electoral districts. Can you sort of walk us through that reporting?

Parker: Sure. So the first way we heard about this competition, which was not public, was almost inadvertently. We were speaking with a Cabinet secretary who said that there was an event in New York that they had kind of wanted to attend, but had declined because they didn’t want to get docked points in the competition. And we were immediately like, What competition?

And so it turns out that there is this unofficial travel competition in the Trump White House. It’s overseen by a woman named Meghan Bauer, who basically coordinates with all of the Cabinet secretaries, officially running between Memorial Day and Labor Day. And basically the goal is to encourage Cabinet officials, Cabinet secretaries to travel the country, particularly to swing districts or swing states that are competitive in the midterms. And each time they go to one of these areas, they get a point. And what this Cabinet official was worried about was losing points, although the official was mistaken. When we began reporting, many officials at the White House told us, Nobody ever loses points; you only accrue points. And they even said, Look, if someone is heading to New York to, say, do a hit on CNN, to talk about Trump’s policies, that still would count as a point.

Harris: We can talk about it in point systems, but we should also think of it in terms of the law, right? Like, is this a Hatch Act violation?

Parker: So, no, not inherently, but it brings Cabinet officials potentially quite close to the line, and it’s something they need to be careful of. So just to put it in a little historical perspective, this general thing of wanting your top officials, your Cabinet officials, out in the country selling the president’s policies, especially in the run-up to a midterm election, is incredibly common. [George W.] Bush did it; [Barack] Obama did it; [Joe] Biden did it.

And Biden, I remember, the most in-demand Cabinet official at the time, when he was president in the run-up to the midterms, was Pete Buttigieg. So Cabinet officials can go and they can talk about—especially if it’s related to their jobs, an agriculture secretary, for instance, or let’s just take Pete Buttigieg for an example. Pete Buttigieg could travel the country and talk about how this stimulus package that Biden and Democrats helped to pass had brought a bridge to your district, had brought new roads to your state, was responsible for huge construction projects over here that had created jobs. That’s all totally fine and not a Hatch Act violation.

If it becomes more overtly political—showing up in a district at a campaign stop with, say, a Senate candidate and just saying, Hey, vote for Ken Paxton in Texas—that is where you get into problems. And the Trump officials, some of them have gotten into problems.

Harris: Tom, how do you process the sort of flood, the stream of controversy, that comes from the administration?

Nichols: Well, I actually am intimately familiar with the Hatch Act because people filed complaints against me constantly when I was a federal employee, before I came to The Atlantic. I was a professor at the Naval War College, which meant I was a Defense Department employee, but I wrote articles and I wrote op-eds and I spoke my mind. And I always finish with, These are my personal views, speaking as an American citizen, et cetera, et cetera.

So I think Ashley’s description of, boy, right up to the line, is a great way to think of it. And the larger point, I think, is that, Adam, like you asked: Why does this happen? How do we cope with this flood? And I think that the flood is the point. The fire hose is the point, because at some point, you just sort of throw up your hands and say, Which of these, you know, 9 million things?

It used to be that, even in the first Trump term, somebody getting hit with a Hatch Act violation was a big deal. I mean, it made the news. Kellyanne Conway, there were couple of other—

Parker: Yeah, I remember the Kellyanne Conway one. And it stood out, right?

Nichols: Yeah, right. Because it was rare. And because it was so obvious. And I think it’s part of that whole fire-hosing strategy, where you just sit back and say, Okay, fine. I give up, because tomorrow there will be something else. And then the Hatch Act will seem relatively minor by comparison.

Parker: I was thinking about this as I was biking into work today, which is, if you even just look at today’s news, Hatch Act violations are comparatively quaint, right? I mean, I’m biking in, I see that ProPublica has reported that a Russian oligarch who’s very close to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin bankrolled Donald Trump Jr.’s intimate wedding a few months ago. And amid all these warnings that AI is going to kill us in a doomsday scenario, President Trump came out and said, We’re not slowing down; there’s no regulations. So if a Cabinet official says, Hey, vote for this Republican congressman, in the panoply of things that watchdog groups are worrying about, it’s not top of the list, to be frank.

Nichols: I know the broken-windows theory of crime has been more or less discredited, but there is a kind of feeling of this of, It starts with the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act is like turnstile jumping in the subway, but enough people do it enough times and pretty soon, you know, it’s people shooting at each other in the streets and robbing banks. And it kind of feels that way now. There are no guardrails.

I mean, the story that Ashley just mentioned, about Don Jr.’s wedding. Again, if you were a federal employee, if you even talked to a Russian, that was paperwork right there. I could not imagine saying, Oh yeah, and by the way, he paid for my wedding. But we’ve just kind of gotten used to it.

Harris: Republicans gathered in Dallas, Texas, last week for a sort of unusual midterm convention. What did we learn about where Republicans are right now, if anything, coming out of that convention?

Nichols: We learned that the party belongs to Donald Trump and that thousands of people will repeat every word he says if he tells them to. That, I think, tells you everything you need to know—about the party, not about the election, but about the party.

Parker: I think that’s about right, because a lot of Republicans did not think this was a good use of time or money. If you’re actually focused on winning the midterms, they wanted to be campaigning in their districts, in their states—let alone for some of them, depending on the district or the state, aligning themselves with a president who’s quite unpopular and whose policies are quite unpopular. But nonetheless, you still saw a number of them travel to Dallas despite not really wanting to, because as Tom said, Trump is the leader of this party and he demanded a midterm convention, so he got one.

Harris: I was, as I was watching it go on, thinking about what was driving the news as we were heading into the convention, which was this sort of burgeoning trade war with Canada.

Trump himself mentioned Canada briefly during the convention, saying—

Donald Trump: Canada very much wants to make a deal. They’re dying to make a deal.

Harris: Tom, that’s all well and good, but the reality is that the president has chosen to squabble with one of America’s closest allies. Where do things stand now between the U.S. and Canada? And is there any sense of a thawing? Or do you think things are continuing to heat up?

Nichols: Well, first, let’s always point out that the president’s default response to any controversy is that Country X is desperate to make a deal. It’s literally Donald Trump’s Mad Lib—one of the Mad Lib sentences. You know, What do you think about the controversy with Country X? The answer is always, Controversy will be over soon. Country X is begging to make a deal. They’re calling me every day, whether it’s Canada, Iran, the Houthis, you name it.

I think the Canadians have simply decided they’ve had enough of this nonsense. They are no longer partners; they are adversaries in the economic space. But I think that the Canadians have said, Fine.

A majority of the Canadians don’t want to pay for this Trump–Carney tariff war, but they support Carney standing up to Trump. And so my guess is this is not retrievable until Trump is gone from office, which is a real tragedy, even if Trump backs down from the tariffs, which he almost certainly is going to do sooner rather than later, I think.

Harris: Yeah. And as you mentioned, right, Carney’s approval rating is quite high. Ashley, how has he been responding to the president, and how has the back-and-forth been going in recent days?

Parker: Well, I sort of understand Carney in his response going back to a speech he gave much earlier this year at Davos, where he basically said, The world order as we—I’m paraphrasing here—the world order as we know it is over. And all of these sort of smaller countries have always supplicated themselves to the United States for protection or for deals or for various reasons, and that’s no longer a good strategy for us. And so I think Carney’s response in this trade war is him sort of acting on those principles he laid out at Davos. And one thing that was so striking to me when you look at the back-and-forth—and it looks like both sides had issues; it’s hard to point specifically to which side blew up the most recent deal—but one thing that comes through is Trump has talked about wanting Canada to be a 51st state, and that mainly seems to be trolling, except not entirely; there’s always a kernel of truth with everything Trump does.

But in these negotiations, it feels like the American side has sort of internalized the idea that Canada is less a sovereign nation and more a 51st state. And when you look at the terms that Canada objected to, it was stuff the United States negotiators demanded, which would be reasonable if Canada was a state, but is not reasonable if Canada is a sovereign nation and an ally to our north. And it feels like that’s where things fell apart.

Harris: Tom, actually in your piece the other day, you talked about the way that the president doesn’t view other nations as sovereign nations. There’s just this idea that he can’t go in and extract things in the way that he would if it were just a part of something that he already owned. Can you sort of flesh out that idea a little bit?

Nichols: Well, I mean, not to psychoanalyze the president from a distance, but I think most people would agree the president’s a pretty narcissistic guy. He’s got to put his name on everything. He builds monuments to himself. Every sentence begins with I. And people like that don’t think of other people as real people; they think of them as players on the stage that surrounds them. And I think that’s very clear with Donald Trump.

This convention, going back to the convention we were mentioning, you know, he doesn’t really think of other people trying to win elections, and he doesn’t care. They’re supposed to come to his big party and wear a hat and bring noisemakers and that’s it. And that’s the extent of his interest. And I think that’s how he is with foreign countries, that he says they’re all kind of wholly or partially owned subsidiaries of Donald Trump Incorporated. He doesn’t think of them as real places with unique cultures or particular interests led by human beings who may not actually see the world the way he does or care about his interests as much as he cares about his interests.

And that’s partly why you always get these kind of stock answers of They’re gonna make a deal, because of course everybody makes a deal, because that’s what I want. And they’re gonna do what I tell them to do, because of course, all my life, everyone has done what I tell them to do.

It flummoxes him completely when a foreign nation says, We’re not going to do that. And one of the reasons—you know, I don’t want to extend this analogy by Canada too far—but I think that’s one of the reasons he’s having such a hard time with the war of choice he began in Iran. He just can’t imagine that—he says, I demand that you do X, Y, and Z. And the Iranians say, No and here’s a bunch of missiles and drones as part of that answer. And I think he totally unravels him, because he’s just never had to deal with that.

And I think when Mark Carney, you know, as Ashley was saying, Who is this uppity governor, to speak to the president in this way?, instead of the leader of a sovereign nation and place that’s part of NATO and has real interests in the world—one of our second or third biggest trading partners. He cannot internalize that. It doesn’t make it—it’s not like he rejects the idea. It’s like he can’t grasp the idea.

Parker: And just to briefly follow on Tom, I mean, Trump has such legitimate faith and confidence in himself as a dealmaker that he really can’t fathom that. You may recall that when he was campaigning, he said, On day one, the war between Russia and Ukraine will end, which is a sort of promise presidents make—day one signals it’s a priority. But in talking to Trump’s aides, they’re like, No, no; he actually thought that. Like, he actually thought that he was such a good dealmaker, it would end. And obviously it hasn’t.

Harris: When we come back, we talk about the danger of AI, and Ashley and Tom talk about what they’ll be reporting on in the week ahead.

[Music]

Harris: I wanna switch gears a little bit, speaking of the idea of things that people can and cannot control. Over the last several days, CEOs of leading AI companies have been sounding the alarm, really in a lot of the same ways that Bill Gates, when he was on the show with Hanna [Rosin] not that long ago, was talking about the growing risks of artificial intelligence and the products and the ways that people are using those products.

Trump doesn’t appear to be heeding those concerns and has responded that the U.S. has to, quote, “win AI.”

What is your reaction to this, to all of this?

Nichols: That’s a classic Trump answer. You know, We have to win AI. That’s the president’s way of saying, I didn’t understand the question. I don’t really know what this is, and so we just have to win it. Because that’s a good kind of standard. You could have filled in anything: What do you think about the, you know, international chocolate-milk market?



Well, we have to win that.

Parker: Yeah, is winning AI, we die first?

Nichols: Yeah. (Laughs.) What does that mean?

Parker: I will confess, I don’t fully understand all of the intricacies of AI either, but from what I do understand, to be somewhat fair to Trump, or to anyone, is that this is just fundamentally incredibly complex. And, you know, lawmakers, one problem you have is if you’ve ever watched these members of Congress—which is basically a gerontocracy—try to get to the bottom of Snapchat or Instagram or social media with teens, right, it’s like they’re speaking a foreign language. And those are table stakes, right? AI is a million times more complicated than posting a problematic video on YouTube or Instagram.

So first of all, a lot of the people in the United States responsible for possibly regulating this are like me, which is terrifying—can’t begin to possibly understand the nuances or the complexities. And the second thing is, even if the United States is willing to regulate, the question is you would sort of need a mutually-assured-destruction pact with China and with other countries. This is a sort of globalized problem.
